rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology <U+2013> case study with semi-structured interviews (19 farmers, WUA presidents/secretaries, officials), policy document analysis and field observations. Q2: Transformation 2 and Figure 2 <U+2013> 1371 ha of former rain-fed slopes converted to drip (38.9% of irrigated area); Transformation 3 and Table 1 <U+2013> shift to citrus/kaki monoculture with higher crop water requirements; Discussion <U+2013> combination of drip, area expansion and intensification led to more water use at watershed level. Q3: expansion established by official municipal land statistics (Figure 2, Table 1) and independently by stakeholder interviews (WUA president in Montesa describing expansion up the hills after well permit). Q4: intermediate variables documented <U+2013> irrigated area expansion (1371 ha), crop shift to citrus (76% of irrigated produce in Montesa) with IVIA irrigation requirements (4114 m3/ha citrus vs 2053 vineyard), and 88.2% of area now groundwater-fed. Q6: result reported at watershed level across four municipalities. Q7: Transformation 1 and 2 <U+2013> expansion required basin authority concessions for wells and sufficient water availability; lower municipalities expanded most because they had water, while La Font de la Figuera could not expand as wells dried. Q8: Transformations section and Conclusions <U+2013> transformations cannot be solely attributed to drip irrigation, also relate to broader changes in Spanish agriculture.
rows.notes: Water consumption increase is not measured; it is inferred from area expansion and crop water requirement tables (IVIA, Allen et al.). The study's own evidence concerns expansion and crop intensification accompanying drip; the consumptive-use conclusion is deduced. No dispersion statistics (Q9).

rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology <U+2013> own interviews, document analysis and field observations in four municipalities. Q2: Transformation 5 <U+2013> canals used before the shift to drip abandoned or disused, only one ancient weir in Montesa still operational, mills, pools and underground canals in Vallada abandoned; interview quotes from WUA secretary (Vallada) and president (Moixent) on unmaintained weir and destroyed Moorish canal. Q4: documents that surface irrigation now covers only 413 ha (11.7%) and 88.2% of irrigated area is groundwater-fed, so canals no longer needed; farmers cannot cope with maintenance costs and administration has a non-conservation attitude. Q6: reported across the four villages of the watershed. Q7: Transformation 5 <U+2013> loss occurs because farmers cannot afford maintenance costs and the public administration does not prioritise water heritage, contrasted with maintained canals elsewhere (Hermosilla 2010). Q8: Transformations introduction and Conclusions <U+2013> impacts not solely attributable to drip irrigation.
rows.notes: Heritage loss is supported mainly by interview statements; the field observation component is not explicitly distinguished from interview and literature sources, so triangulation is doubtful (Q3 no). Q4 mechanism is partly asserted; the quantified part is the shrinkage of surface-irrigated area. No uncertainty measures.

notes: Full text appears complete. Qualitative case study (interviews n~44 plus official statistics); no quantitative measurements of water consumption or dispersion statistics.
